name: The Landlord's Game, live again
description: A practice: Lizzie Magie's game of 1904 (public domain), rebuilt as data with both of her rule sets, the landlord's way and Prosperity. Board layout, names and amounts are ours.
rights_note: The game itself is public domain (US patents 748,626 of 1904 and 1,509,312 of 1924). These words, names and numbers: PlayfulProcess, CC BY-SA 4.0.

sections.What it is: Start. Each time you pass, the land pays wages: $100.
Land in use. Buy it if it is free; the price goes into the Public Treasury. Lot 1 of 22, price $60.
sections.The landlord's way: Landing pays rent to the owner (30% of the price); three lots on one side double it.
sections.Prosperity: Landing pays ground rent into the Public Treasury; buying it gives every other player $10.

sections.Rules: The player with the least money goes first. Roll two dice and move; passing or landing on Mother Earth pays $100 wages and counts a lap. Buy free lots, railroads and franchises, paying the price into the Public Treasury; others pay you when they land. Three lots on a side double their rent. Necessities cost $20 to the Public Treasury. Luxuries: a $50 ticket worth $60 at the end, or lose a turn. No Trespassing sends you to Jail: each turn roll; doubles free you, otherwise pay $50 and move or stay; the third roll without doubles pays. Short of cash, sell land of your choice back to the bank at half price; short of that, the Poorhouse, and you are out. When every player still in has been round five times, or one player is left, the richest wins: cash, land at its price and $60 a ticket.
sections.Source: After US patent 748,626 (Magie, 1904), public domain: the price paid into the Public Treasury, the $60 luxury ticket, Jail by doubles or a $50 fine, and the end at the fifth pass of Mother Earth are hers. Choosing what to sell is from the 1924 patent. Amounts and names are ours.

sections.Rules: Same board, dice, wages and Jail; the price of a lot goes into the Public Treasury. Ground rent goes to the Public Treasury too (the single tax). A luxury is $50 into the Treasury, with no ticket. Railroads and franchises are public ($10 fare). A new lot in use gives every other player $10. Passing Mother Earth, the Treasury pays half its balance to all players equally. The Poorhouse is a waiting room: your land goes back to the bank, you still share in the payouts, and you leave from Mother Earth with $50. Everyone wins together when the player who started with the least has doubled it and holds at least as much as anyone, while nobody holds less than they started with: the poorest rises to the top, and nobody falls. With equal starts every player must double (the harder table). If every player has been round five times first, the table loses: talk about why.
sections.Source: The poorest player's doubling is the win as reported by Ketcham (Harper's, 2012) and Pilon (The Monopolists, 2015); 'as much as anyone' and 'nobody below their start' are ours (October 2026), so the table can lose. Magie's revision is US patent 1,509,312 (1924), published 1932 as The Landlord's Game and Prosperity. Amounts are ours.

sections.Story: Patent applied for in 1903, granted January 5, 1904. Published by Georgists in 1906; Parker Brothers declined it in 1909. Revised and patented in 1924; published in 1932 with Prosperity. Darrow sold Monopoly to Parker Brothers in 1935; that year Magie sold them her patent for $500. She disputed his claim in 1936 and died in 1948.
sections.The question: After one game each way: which felt more exciting, and why?
